text: If 2 Maccabees 7:28 is not teaching the
doctrine of creation ex nihilo or
creation out of nothing, what is it
teaching?
Hey everybody, I'm Dan McClellan. I'm a
scholar of the Bible and religion. And
if you're not familiar with 2 Maccabees,
it's a part of the Apocrypha. It's a
fascinating book that narrates the
Maccabean revolt against the oppression
of Antiochus the Fourth Epiphanes, the
Seleucid ruler. Now, chapter 7 is
probably the most famous chapter of the
whole book, and in this chapter,
Antiochus captures a mother and her
seven sons, and then one by one tries to
force them to eat pork. And they refuse,
and the mother is exhorting them one by
one to remain faithful. And this story
actually has its own history. Goes back
to some other traditions. There's a man
named Tajo, for instance, who has seven
sons, and more or less the same thing
happens. And then you also see it in 4
Maccabees. But, in verse 28, we see this
Greek passage. And I'm not going to read
the Greek here, but here is the English
translation from the New English
Translation of the Septuagint. I implore
you, my child, to look at the heaven and
the earth and see everything that is in
them,
and recognize that God did not make them
out of things that existed.
And in the same way, the human race came
into being.
Now, it certainly seems like this could
be talking about creation out of
nothing, and there are a lot of people
who very, very firmly believe it does.
And that's not what it's talking about.
And one of the clearest indicators is
that
the way they're talking about the
creation of the universe parallels the
way the human race was brought into
being. And even according to the Bible,
the human race was not created ex
nihilo. Humanity, according to Genesis
2, was created from the dust of the
earth. And humanity, according to
Genesis 1, was just created. It doesn't
say how. But, this is not creation out
of nothing. This is creation out of
something.
So, what's going on here with this out
of things that didn't exist, or not out
of things that did exist? Well, here's
the Greek again. I've underlined the
relevant portion, ouk ex ontōn epiesen
autō theos. And this basically says,
"Not out of being things, or the being,
he made them God." So, let's take a look
at this phrase and cognate phrases. And
by cognate, I mean other phrases that
use different words, but are saying the
same thing in some other earlier
literature, so we can get a grasp of
what's actually going on here. And I'm
going to start with
a
late 5th century BCE text by an author
named Xenophon. And the text is the
Memorabilia. And in Memorabilia, book 2,
chapter 2, section 3, we have this
underlined Greek, hōs egonēs ek men ouk
ontōn epiesen einai. And ek men ouk
ontōn is grammatically synonymous with
what we saw in 2 Maccabees 7. Now, the
translation in the Loeb Classical
Library is pretty interpretive. It's
from, I think, 1923, and it really just
paraphrases, and not in a very precise
way. Here's the English translation, "To
their parents, children owe their
existence." This doesn't really
represent what the Greek says
very closely at all. So, I'm going to go
to a 2001 translation by Amy Bonnett.
And here we see a much more literal
translation, "Their parents caused them
to come from non-being to being."
So, this is using more or less the same
phrase to say that parents create their
children in the same way, which is
closely related to how the mother of the
seven sons says that in the same way the
human race came into being. So, what is
this non-being and being stuff language
really all about? Well, this reflects
the conventional philosophical wisdom
from the ancient world regarding the
nature of matter.
There is matter that has form and
function, and there is matter that does
not have form and function. And the
latter
occupies
the realm of non-being. To bring
something into being is to take unformed
or chaotic matter and to impose upon it
form or function.
And then that moves it into the realm of
being.
And then to remove or divest it of its
form and function is to return it to the
realm of non-being. And we can see this
rather explicitly in Aristotle in a text
called Generation of Animals, or On the
Generation of Animals. Here we see the
Greek that uses
ek tou me ontos toward the beginning of
the second line. And this is, again,
grammatically synonymous, even though
it's using slightly different words.
But, here's the translation from the LCL
of what Aristotle is saying here. "The
process of formation, genesis, starts
from not being and advances till it
reaches being. That of decay starts from
being and goes back again till it
reaches not being." So, the idea here is
the same as in Xenophon and appears to
be the same as what's in 2 Maccabees
That God created from this unformed
material substrate
the earth. And it's the same idea in 2
Maccabees 7:28 with the creation of the
human race. Something that did not have
form and function was given form and
function, and that brought into being
the human race. Similarly, parents
create children by taking material that
does not have form and function, or at
least a form and function that is
entirely distinct from what it will
become, which, in the case of Xenophon,
is children. But, I think you could
compare it to a cake.
I can have all the ingredients of a
cake, but there's no cake.
And so, when I combine all those
ingredients together, and we have the
mechanical and we have the other kinds
of changes that go on, suddenly
a cake comes into being, not out of
nothing, but out of things that were not
a cake. So, this is the conventional
wisdom of the ancient world all the way
up until the late 2nd century CE.
This is where Christians are engaging
with
Greek thinkers and Gnostics and others
about the one morality of eternal
matter, and two, the rationality of the
resurrection. Because you have some
people who are mocking Christians for
believing that anyone would want to muck
around for eternity in the pigsty of
material, fleshly, corporeal existence.
Cuz that was considered in this time
period to be pretty base and to be
unwanted. And we wanted to transcend the
fleshly and the material and return to
become one with the pleroma, the
fullness. And in the course of that
debate, it became useful to just assert
that, "Well, God created the universe
out of nothing." And this is something
that had been entirely rejected up until
the late 2nd century CE. Out of nothing,
nothing comes. That was the conventional
wisdom. And so, once this doctrine had
been created, Christians looked back on
2 Maccabees 7:28 and a passage in Romans
and a passage in Hebrews and elsewhere,
and they said, "Ah,
that's our doctrine. That's creation out
of nothing." And so, now that we had
this new interpretive lens of creation
out of nothing, the passages that
previously had very clearly not been
about creation out of nothing and that
directly paralleled the views of
Xenophon and Aristotle and many, many
others, now those things could be reread
as references to creation out of
nothing. And the Christians who had just
created this doctrine, or had been
living when the doctrine was created,
could now feel like it had been there
all along. And that served their
rhetorical goals, their rhetorical
interests, and that became the
understanding of passages like 2
Maccabees 7:28. And so, for folks who
have looked through the interpretive
lenses of
these passages are creation out of
nothing, creation ex nihilo, for their
entire lives,
it can be difficult to overcome
those intuitions. It can be difficult to
acknowledge the existence of those
lenses and the influence of those lenses
and remove them. But, if you sincerely
want to know what the experts think is
going on in these texts, it's not
creation ex nihilo. It's the bringing of
unformed matter from the realm of
non-being into being, giving form and
function to that matter, creating
something new, not out of nothing, but
out of something different, similar to
how God creates humanity in the Hebrew
Bible, similar to how parents create
children.
It is taking something that is not a
child or not humanity, giving it a form
and a function that turns it into a
child or humanity. So, 2 Maccabees 7:28
is not preaching or teaching creation ex
nihilo. It's talking about creation out
of existing matter. And for more
discussion on the philosophical
underpinnings of all this, I'd highly
recommend this 1995 UPenn doctoral
dissertation by James Huebler, Creation
ex nihilo, matter, creation, and the
body in classical and Christian
philosophy through Aquinas. And then
there's also, of course, Gerhard Mayes'
wonderful book Creation Ex Nihilo, the
English translation of the original
German was published, I believe, in the
early to mid-90s. So, that's what 2
Maccabees 7:28 is talking about when it
says that the universe was created not
out of things that existed. And the fit
for this video has been the throwback
Broncos.
